A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MSSR framework and SOG module. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original MMSI-Bench and ViewSpatial-Bench evaluations, component ablations, inference measurements, and a fine-tuning experiment using MSSR-generated traces.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds backbone comparisons, perception-module and noise analyses, failure analysis, and ScanQA/SQA3D evaluations.

M1.justification: The dual-agent acquisition, pruning, and requesting loop, execution-state preservation, and coarse-to-fine SOG procedure are retained. Module implementations match between v1 Appendix B and v2 Appendix C. New prompt/API descriptions disclose implementation details; the proposed Verification Agent remains future work.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained MMSI-Bench and ViewSpatial-Bench coverage, v2 Appendix G adds actual evaluations on ScanQA and SQA3D. These extend coverage to object-centric and situated question answering in pre-scanned indoor environments, with answer requirements different from the original multiple-choice evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the earlier comparators and adds Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, Video-3D-LLM, LLaVA-3D, and VLM-3R, including a dedicated 3D-VLM comparison group. The new ScanQA/SQA3D comparison also includes Gemini-1.5-Flash and Gemini-1.5-Pro, distinct from the original Gemini 2.5 comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces uniform and mixed PA/RA backbone configurations, 16-frame inputs and a 2-shot comparison setting for ScanQA/SQA3D with CIDEr and EM@1, controlled perception-noise levels, and manual inspection of half the failure cases. These are added evaluation designs; the original fine-tuning settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 extends component ablations to ViewSpatial-Bench and adds backbone sensitivity, individual perception-module removals, depth/localization/orientation corruption tests, and a ViewSpatial iteration analysis. Appendices H–I add categorized failures and five illustrated failure cases, substantially expanding diagnosis beyond v1's minimality and framework-component studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added failure percentages are descriptive results, and the Gaussian noise magnitudes define experimental perturbations rather than uncertainty estimates for performance.

E6.justification: Original headline accuracies remain 49.5% on MMSI-Bench and 51.8% on ViewSpatial-Bench; fine-tuned Qwen accuracy remains 30.1%. Numerous results are added, including 39.8% MMSI accuracy with Qwen2.5-VL-7B agents and ScanQA/SQA3D scores of 32.49/27.40. Some additions are inconsistent: Table 7 gives 51.8% for MMSI-Bench, and several Table 9 drops disagree with its accuracy values.

T1.justification: Appendix E newly defines stochastic corruption models using multiplicative Gaussian depth noise and additive Gaussian position noise. The MSS sufficiency/minimality definitions and reconstruction, calibration, and SOG mathematics are otherwise retained; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: minimal-sufficient information construction, a dual-agent framework with SOG, leading performance on the two original benchmarks, and useful reasoning traces for supervision. Additional evaluations support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of agent-specific backbone sensitivity, computational tradeoffs, perception bottlenecks, noise sensitivity, and lexical evaluation bias. Its revised limitations distinguish logical from numerical perception errors and propose future verification, replacing v1's broader discussion of error accumulation and benchmark limitations. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix G claims superiority over GPT-o3 on ScanQA despite Table 10 showing otherwise.

D1.justification: New Appendix B supplies a PA prompt template, an API signature/docstring example with argument shapes, and details of injecting module instances into the Python execution namespace. Appendix H newly describes forced decisions at the iteration limit. Existing hardware, fine-tuning hyperparameters, module implementations, and code-access statements are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for ScanQA, VLM-3R, Video-3D-LLM, LLaVA-3D, and a Qwen3 technical report, broadening comparison with recent 3D models. Section 2's related-work discussion and the central positioning against accumulative agentic approaches remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most retained prose is nearly verbatim. v2 inserts a backbone-evaluation subsection, expands the appendix organization, rewrites the limitations discussion, and updates affiliation, contribution, and publication-header text. Wording and cross-reference edits are limited rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds a backbone table, five appendix tables, a ViewSpatial iteration plot, five illustrated failure cases, and two code listings. Table 1 gains rows and a comparison category; Table 2 gains a ViewSpatial column. Existing diagrams and execution traces are retained and relocated within the conference layout.

improvement.justification: The added backbone/component studies, failure analysis, and PA interface documentation improve coverage and reproducibility. However, material reporting problems weaken several additions: Table 7 conflicts with the retained MMSI accuracy; Table 9 reports a 2.3-point drop for 49.5 to 45.2, among other incorrect differences; and Appendix G claims to beat GPT-o3 although Table 10 gives 32.49 versus 33.30. The PDFs do not resolve whether these are isolated transcription errors or broader analytical problems, preventing a confident net-quality judgment.
